result.summary:
Lens: Windows PowerShell 5.1 and Windows file semantics, applied to the uncommitted delta in windows11_guest.ps1, windows11_bootstrap.ps1, test_windows11_guest_driver.py, check_portability.py and python-test-inventory.v1.json. I found no blocking defect. The tests pass (35 passed), and the two WINDOWS11_NATIVE_PINS match the working-tree sha256 values (6805076b… and a188d35e…). Both scripts are pure ASCII.

What I checked:
- **Here-string and backticks:** the attestor sits inside a single-quoted @' '@ here-string, so `"`r`n"` is written to disk literally. The attestor then runs it as a double-quoted string, which produces CRLF. The apostrophe in "guest's" does not end the here-string, because only a line that starts with '@ does.
- **File sharing:** in .NET Framework, File.AppendAllText opens with StreamWriter(path, true, enc), which is FileMode.Append, FileAccess.Write, FileShare.Read. The guest opens with FileAccess.Read and FileShare.ReadWrite|Delete. These are compatible whichever process opens first, and the attestor's Remove-Item at its start still succeeds while the guest holds its handle.
- **Trace failures:** TraceStep's own try/catch swallows a failed append, which is a terminating MethodInvocationException under ErrorActionPreference Stop. Because the function runs in its own scope, the outer catch's `$_` is not touched before the attestor writes its error receipt.
- **Scheduled task:** `New-ScheduledTaskSettingsSet -ExecutionTimeLimit (New-TimeSpan -Minutes 10)` is valid. The scheduler kills the process, which closes its handles, and the per-line open/close appends keep every completed step in the trace.
- **Get-Item:** on a missing path, `Get-Item -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` writes only a non-terminating error and returns `$null`, even under Stop and StrictMode. FileInfo.Length is cached by the provider's Exists check. The standard user has read access through the inherited Users ReadAndExecute ACE, and round 35 showed the fixture user reading both the SYSTEM-written trace and machine.json.
- **Partial or missing receipts:** an empty, partial or locked receipt fails inside ProtectedReceipt's try and returns `$null`. This covers ConvertFrom-Json errors and a Get-Content sharing violation against the writer's handle, which I believe Set-Content opens with FileShare.Write. PS 5.1's JavaScriptSerializer leaves ISO date strings as strings, so the boot_time string comparison is sound.
- **Wait loop:** `break` inside if-blocks within the do/while exits the loop, and the limit is an absolute time on `$clock`. The current receipt is read before the error file, and the error only ends the wait early when MachineDiffers finds its schema, nonce and boot all match. An error written with a null nonce or boot does not end the wait and is still retained.
- **Trace read and copy:** `$traceBytes.Length-$traceCount` parses as subtraction. The read loop stops at EOF or when the 65537-byte buffer is full, and the over-64 KB refusal precedes a CreateNew write.
- **Host side:** the result-member cap is 100 and a passing run produces about 42 files. Member-name validation accepts attestor-trace.txt, and the host's 3300 s work deadline easily covers the longer wait.
- **One run per boot:** round 35's diagnostic trace was appended and never cleared, and it shows a single "started" line in a boot that included OOBE. That supports the KI's assumption of one logon per boot. The residuals the KI already lists are real but out of reach in a one-logon campaign: a stale same-boot error ending the wait, the trace removed between Test-Path and Open, and the same race in the receipt-retention loop. Under this delta's every-250-ms polling there is also a possible collision between the guest's read handle (no FileShare.Delete) and the attestor's start-of-run Remove-Item. I did not report these.

The one remaining issue is non-blocking: whether the 150 s wait leaves enough of the 300 s guest budget. The claim that it leaves half is not established, and the test that pins it cannot fail. The outcome would be a fail-closed deadline FAIL, not a wrong pass, a hang or lost evidence.

I did not edit any repository files or write any scratch files.

findings.claim: The machine-receipt wait is measured from when the wait starts, not from guest start. It therefore leaves 300 - S - 150 s, not 'half of the guest's 300 s work deadline', where S is the time spent before the wait. Neither the comment, the KI-0175 text nor the new test establishes that the remaining time is enough for the rest of the run inside the Windows 11 VM. An attestor that writes a valid receipt late in the window would likely turn into a later 'Guest work deadline exceeded' FAIL in a lifecycle phase. That outcome fails closed but is wrong.
findings.evidence: Guest lines 343-347: "150 s tolerates that variance and leaves half of the guest's 300 s work deadline for the phases that follow" followed by `$machineLimit=$clock.Elapsed.TotalSeconds+150`. `$clock` starts at line 4, and before the wait the guest hashes every seed file including windows-portable.zip (lines 330-334), Add-Types the 53,069-byte windows11_owned.cs (line 337) and runs Get-CimInstance (line 338). A cold first-logon WMI would slow this step in exactly the case where the attestor is slow. After the wait, dxdiag can take up to 45 s with no budget check (`if(-not $dx.WaitEmpty(45000))`, line 409), the host accept can take up to 15 s (line 425), then come ZIP extraction (line 434), six launches and five framed QMP accepts. The only lifecycle timing on record is from hosted Windows Server 2025, not a Windows 11 VM: 64.6-69.4 s for the sliced phases only, without dxdiag, the environment accept, frame accepts or extraction (docs/evidence/m03-native-runtime-diagnostics/README.md, rounds 21/23/26). The comparable GNOME VM lifecycle took 340.6 s (round 28). The new test pins the margin with a constant comparison that can never fail: `assert int(budget.group(1)) - 150 >= 150`. KI-0175 repeats the claim: "The guest waits up to 150 s, half of its 300 s work deadline."
findings.suggested_fix: Make the bound absolute on the guest clock, `$machineLimit=150`, so the wait ends at the 150 s mark whatever S is and 150 s of budget always remain. This also makes the comment and the KI wording true. Alternatively, correct the comment, KI and test to say 'at most 150 s after pre-wait setup', and retain `$clock.ElapsedMilliseconds` at the end of the wait in the proof so a late receipt followed by a deadline FAIL can be attributed. Either way, the test should not stand in for a measured post-attestation duration in the VM.

result.summary:
Security, privacy and fail-closed review of the uncommitted delta to windows11_guest.ps1, windows11_bootstrap.ps1, test_windows11_guest_driver.py, check_portability.py and python-test-inventory.v1.json. No repository file was edited. The 35/35 tests in test_windows11_guest_driver.py pass.

Two non-blocking findings:

1. **The trace privacy guard can be bypassed (SEC-1).** It matches PowerShell names case-sensitively and does not check aliases. Three mutants survive all 35 tests:
   - a lowercase `tracestep` call that writes the Winlogon DefaultPassword to the trace;
   - a `$STEP=` assignment that puts the observed user name in the trace;
   - an `sv step` assignment that does the same.

2. **A stale trace can be kept as this run's (SEC-2).** The trace is not tied to a nonce, boot or logon. The new per-iteration Get-Content poll of machine-error.json does not share Delete, so it can collide with the attestor's Remove-Item of that file, which runs before the try. That can stop the next attestor run before it removes an earlier logon's trace, and the guest then keeps that trace. This only happens after an earlier logon left an error receipt, and it always fails closed.

Verified clean in the current code:
- **Trace content.** Every TraceStep argument is a literal or `$step`. `$step` is only ever one of ten fixed names, and the time is `[DateTime]::UtcNow.ToString('o')`. No secret, registry value, user name, machine-specific value or other read value reaches the trace or its retained copy.
- **Early end of the wait.** The wait ends early on an error only when that error matches the error schema, this nonce and this boot. Errors from another nonce, another boot or another schema keep the wait going. An error from an earlier logon in the same boot can still end it; that residual is already documented and fails closed.
- **No failure can pass.** After an early end on an error, `$machine` is null or not current, so the decision block always throws. The pin checks after it are unchanged.
- **Bounded read.** The trace read is truly bounded: a 65,537-byte buffer, a throw above 64 KiB, and the copy opened with CreateNew. It happens before the decision.
- **Permissions.** The harness folder has a protected ACL: SYSTEM and Administrators have full control, and Users only read and execute, inherited by every file. A standard user cannot create, change or delete the trace or either receipt. The attestor's append (AppendAllText shares Read) and the guest's read (shares ReadWrite and Delete) do not block each other.
- **Pins and inventory.** The WINDOWS11_NATIVE_PINS values match the SHA-256 of both files. The inventory count (3173), sort order and digest are consistent.

Pre-existing and outside the delta: the attestor's interactive-user error message includes the observed user name of this synthetic VM. It is written to machine-error.json and kept in the proof.

findings.claim: The new privacy guard for attestor-trace.txt matches PowerShell names case-sensitively and does not cover aliases. PowerShell resolves command and variable names case-insensitively, so a read value, including the Winlogon DefaultPassword, can be routed into the trace (and from there into the retained proof) while all 35 tests still pass. The test comment says every call form, writer and step assignment is covered, and that is false. The shipped attestor code itself does not leak anything today.
findings.evidence: Guard lines: L1415 `calls = re.findall(r"\bTraceStep (\([^)\n]*\)|'[^'\n]*'|\$\w+)", text)`, L1428 `assert len(re.findall(r"\bTraceStep\b", text)) == 1 + len(calls)`, L1442 `assert len(re.findall(r"\$step\s*\+?=", text)) == len(ATTESTOR_STEPS)`, L1443 `for forbidden in ("$script:step", "Set-Variable", "[ref]$step", "${step}"):`. Each mutant was applied to a scratch copy of windows11_bootstrap.ps1 and run with the unchanged test file. All three gave `35 passed`. (m2) Inserted before `Remove-ItemProperty ... DefaultPassword`: `tracestep ([string](Get-ItemProperty -LiteralPath $winlogon).DefaultPassword)`. Lowercase `tracestep` still runs TraceStep in PowerShell and writes the plaintext autologon password to the trace. (m1) `if($system.UserName -cne (...)) { $STEP=[string]$system.UserName; throw (...) }`. `$STEP` is the same variable as `$step`, so the catch's `TraceStep ('caught at '+$step)` writes the user name. (m3) The same with `sv step ([string]$system.UserName)`. Scratch copies: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-tanishkalwad-jobapplyv2/17ee071f-b2d5-4e6f-a57e-209b35ae06c1/scratchpad/fix6/review-security/m1, m2, m3. This also contradicts the KI-0175 note in KNOWN_ISSUES that every reviewer mutant routing a read value into the trace was killed.
findings.suggested_fix: Compile the guard regexes with re.IGNORECASE: TraceStep calls and count, the $step assignment patterns, $tracePath, [IO.File]::, AppendAllText, the writer cmdlet list and the ${step} form. Then require every case-insensitive occurrence of the token `step` used as a variable or variable name (`$step`, `${step}`, `-Name step`, `sv step`, `Set-Variable`/`New-Variable`/`nv`/`sv`/`PSVariable`) to be one of the pinned statements. Add m1, m2 and m3 as recorded mutants.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding holds against the current source. In test_attestor_trace_lines_carry_only_step_names_and_timestamps (scripts/tests/test_windows11_guest_driver.py, about L1415-1444), every guard regex and substring check is case-sensitive. That covers `\bTraceStep (...)`, the `\bTraceStep\b` count, `\$step=([^;\n]*)`, `\$step\s*\+?=`, `$tracePath`, `[IO.File]::`, AppendAllText, the writer list, and the forbidden list ("$script:step", "Set-Variable", "[ref]$step", "${step}"). The forbidden list names no aliases. In Windows PowerShell 5.1, function and variable names are resolved case-insensitively, and `sv` is a built-in alias for Set-Variable.

I checked the three scratch mutants under /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-tanishkalwad-jobapplyv2/17ee071f-b2d5-4e6f-a57e-209b35ae06c1/scratchpad/fix6/review-security/:
- m1: `$STEP=[string]$system.UserName` before the throw.
- m2: `tracestep ([string](Get-ItemProperty -LiteralPath $winlogon).DefaultPassword)`, inserted just before Remove-ItemProperty.
- m3: `sv step ([string]$system.UserName)`.

Each differs from the repository bootstrap by that one line, and each test file is byte-identical to the repository's. Running the unchanged test file gave "35 passed" for m1, m2 and m3, the same as the unmodified repository. Each mutant would route a read value into attestor-trace.txt, which the guest keeps in its proof. m1 and m3 do it through the catch's `TraceStep ('caught at '+$step)`; m2 does it directly. So the test comment's claim that every use of TraceStep, every write and every $step assignment is one of the pinned forms is too strong.

The gap is only in test strength, which is why it is non-blocking. The shipped attestor has exactly one lowercase-free TraceStep definition, and its calls pass only fixed literals or $step. $step is assigned only fixed literals, so nothing read reaches the trace today. No campaign would accept a wrong result, no data leaks, nothing hangs, and no repository gate fails: the suite passes and the shipped code is safe.

Side notes:
- The KNOWN_ISSUES KI-0175 sentence ("every reviewer mutant that tried to route a read value into the trace" was killed) refers to the mutants that were actually run, so it is arguably accurate but misleadingly broad.
- The unchanged interactive-user throw already puts the observed user name into the machine-error.json message. That is outside this delta.

The suggested fix is sound: compile the guard regexes with re.IGNORECASE, add alias and variable-cmdlet forms (sv, set, nv, New-Variable, PSVariable, -Name step, ${step} in any case), and record m1, m2 and m3 as killed mutants.

findings.claim: Unlike both receipts, attestor-trace.txt is not tied to a nonce, boot or logon, and the guest keeps whatever trace is present. The delta also makes the guest poll machine-error.json on every loop iteration with Get-Content. This collides with the attestor's Remove-Item of that file, which runs before the try block. If an earlier logon left machine-error.json, the next attestor run can stop on a sharing violation before it writes any receipt and before it removes the earlier trace. The guest then waits the full 150 s and keeps the earlier logon's trace as if it named this run's stalled step. The result always fails closed; no pass is possible. The harm is that the diagnostic this delta adds can point at the wrong run, and the KI-0175 residual list does not mention it.
findings.evidence: Guest L356 (new): `$failed=ProtectedReceipt $machineErrorPath`, inside the 250 ms loop. ProtectedReceipt L119: `try { return (Get-Content -LiteralPath $Path -Raw|ConvertFrom-Json) } ...`. Windows PowerShell 5.1's FileSystem provider opens Get-Content readers with FileShare.ReadWrite, without Delete. This is reasoning from 5.1 behaviour and was not run on the target. Attestor bootstrap L39, outside the try under $ErrorActionPreference='Stop': `if(Test-Path -LiteralPath $errorPath) { Remove-Item -LiteralPath $errorPath -Force }`. L41 removes the trace only after that: `if(Test-Path -LiteralPath $tracePath) { Remove-Item -LiteralPath $tracePath -Force }`. Before the delta, the guest read machine-error.json once, after the deadline. The new trace read correctly shares Delete (`([IO.FileShare]::ReadWrite -bor [IO.FileShare]::Delete)`), but the new error poll does not. Trace lines contain only a UTC time and a step name, and failure.json records neither the guest's boot time nor a wall-clock time, so a reader cannot tell a stale trace apart. Precondition: an earlier logon left an error receipt. This is the same multi-logon case the KI already accepts for a same-boot error ending the wait.
findings.suggested_fix: In the attestor, remove the trace before machine-error.json, or put both removals inside a guarded block, so a failed error removal never leaves an earlier trace in place. Have ProtectedReceipt read through a FileStream that shares ReadWrite|Delete with the same 64 KB bound, as the trace read already does. Have the guest record its own $boot and the UTC time of the trace read next to the retained trace, for example in failure.json or a small guest-written context file, so a stale trace can be recognised. Add this case to the KI-0175 residuals.

verdict.reasoning:
I checked each step of the claim against the current source.

**Bootstrap attestor (windows11_bootstrap.ps1)**
- L39 runs `Remove-Item` on machine-error.json outside the try, with `$ErrorActionPreference='Stop'`.
- L41 removes attestor-trace.txt only after that.
- So if the L39 removal fails, the script ends before it removes the old trace, writes any receipt, or calls TraceStep.

**Guest (windows11_guest.ps1)**
- L356 now calls `ProtectedReceipt $machineErrorPath` on every 250 ms loop iteration. ProtectedReceipt (L116-119) reads the file with `Get-Content -Raw`.
- Before the delta, machine-error.json was read only once, after the deadline (L387).
- In Windows PowerShell 5.1, the FileSystem provider's GetContentReader opens the file with FileShare.ReadWrite and not Delete. While that handle is open, the attestor's delete fails with a sharing violation, and under Stop that is terminating.
- Only the new trace read (L376) shares Delete. Round 36's hosted 5.1 primitives tested a Delete-sharing trace reader, never a Get-Content reader of the error file, so no evidence refutes the collision.

**Other parts of the claim that hold**
- The trace lines carry only a UTC time and a step name.
- failure.json (L480) records no boot time and no wall-clock time.
- The KI-0175 residuals mention only the same-boot early-exit case.
- The result always fails closed: with no current machine.json, every path throws (L384-390).

**Why it is not blocking, and why the precondition is not reachable today**
- The trigger needs a machine-error.json left by an earlier logon. The designed campaign never produces one:
  - The bootstrap creates the harness fresh in specialize and throws if it already exists (L12).
  - The answer file has one AutoLogon.
  - windows11_vm.py does not reboot the guest after logon.
  - The append-only traces from diagnostic rounds 34 and 35 each show exactly one attestor 'started' line.
- Even with a stale file, the race window is narrow. The attestor does its one removal within about 1 s of starting (rounds 34/35/36). The guest reaches its loop only after starting PowerShell, hashing the seed files and running Add-Type.
- In a hit, the outcome is a fail-closed run whose retained diagnostic belongs to the earlier run. It cannot accept a wrong result, leak data, run past the 150 s / 300 s bounds, or fail a repository gate.
- The stated harm is also partly overstated. In the different-boot case, a retained machine-error.json combined with the message 'missing or unreadable' already shows that error was not current. The trace's UTC times can be checked against the host timeline.

**Verdict**
The mechanism is accurate, but its effect is latent and limited to diagnostics. The suggested hardening is cheap: remove the trace first or inside a guarded block, give ProtectedReceipt a Delete-sharing bounded read, and add a KI residual note.

result.summary:
Lens: test adequacy and repository gates. I checked the gates and they hold. No existing assertion was weakened. The new tests do not fully pin the main security invariant, which is that no read value reaches the trace.

Gates I checked directly:
- The pins match the files. `shasum -a 256` gives 6805076b…de2ed1 for windows11_guest.ps1 and a188d35e…e6f3a9 for windows11_bootstrap.ps1, the same as WINDOWS11_NATIVE_PINS. The old hashes appear only under historical docs/evidence. `scripts/check_portability.py` passes.
- The inventory is exact. It is sorted with no duplicates, count 3173 = len(node_ids), and the sha256 matches `_python_inventory_digest`. The bytes equal verify.py's canonical serialization, and posix_only is unchanged. Against HEAD it adds exactly 6 IDs and removes none. Running `--collect-only` on test_windows11_guest_driver.py gives 35 IDs, the same as the inventory.
- `pytest` on the file: 35 passed. Ruff check, ruff format --check and mypy on the changed Python all pass. The other windows11 tests that read these sources (boot_console, host_runtime, isolation) pass 92/92.
- I did not run the full `scripts/verify.py --suite python`.

Weakening check against HEAD: every changed assertion is equal or stricter.
- `text.index("try {")` became `attestor_try`, which asserts exactly one top-level try.
- The wait locator lost its `+30`, but the exact statement list now pins `+150`.
- The order check is extended with `traced`.
- The `[:6]` prefix became an exact `[:8]`.
- The `$machineErrorPath` count went from 2 to 3, matching the new use.
- The HEAD claim that the error file never ends the wait was dropped on purpose. The new invariant, that a current receipt is read first each poll and only a nonce- and boot-bound error breaks, is pinned exactly and also by order.

Mutants: I used the variant.py mirror, with workdirs under /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-tanishkalwad-jobapplyv2/17ee071f-b2d5-4e6f-a57e-209b35ae06c1/scratchpad/fix6/review-tests/m/. These were killed:
- trace copy CreateNew changed to Create
- TraceStep without its try/catch
- task limit back to 1 minute
- unbound early break on the error file
- trace bound `-gt` changed to `-ge`
- trace not removed at run start
- catch traced after writing the error receipt
- wait limit 290
- oversize receipt returning $null

M11 only inserted a line after `$mismatch=@()` and did not actually move the block, so it proves nothing about moving. The `wait < start < decided` order check covers a real move.

The survivors that matter are the three findings below. Mutant IDs in the findings refer to those workdirs.

Two notes outside this delta and lens:
1. No gate parses the attestor body under PS 5.1, because it sits inside a single-quoted here-string. The round-36 diagnostic did parse it for these exact bytes ("parse attestor body", pass), but nothing re-checks future changes.
2. The existing interactive-user throw puts the observed account name into machine-error.json, and the guest copies that file into the proof. Round 36 recorded "observed user: runnervmhao91\\runneradmin".

findings.claim: The test meant to keep secrets out of the trace uses case-sensitive regexes, but PowerShell names are case-insensitive. A one-line attestor change can write the autologon password or the username into attestor-trace.txt, and the guest copies that file into the proof. All 35 tests still pass.
findings.evidence:
The test claims: "Every use of TraceStep, every write and every assignment of $step is one of the above: an unrecognised call form, a second writer or a computed step name would otherwise reach the trace". The checks behind that claim are all case-sensitive, and the scope-prefix deny-list is incomplete:
- `calls = re.findall(r"\bTraceStep (\([^)\n]*\)|'[^'\n]*'|\$\w+)", text)`
- `assert len(re.findall(r"\bTraceStep\b", text)) == 1 + len(calls)`
- `assert len(re.findall(r"\$step\s*\+?=", text)) == len(ATTESTOR_STEPS)`
- `for forbidden in ("$script:step", "Set-Variable", "[ref]$step", "${step}")`
- `for writer in ("Add-Content", ...)`

Mutants that pass all 35 tests:
- M22 inserts `Tracestep ([string](Get-ItemProperty -LiteralPath $winlogon -Name DefaultPassword).DefaultPassword)` before `Remove-ItemProperty ... DefaultPassword`. `Tracestep` resolves to the TraceStep function.
- M21 adds `tracestep ([string]$system.UserName)`.
- These step assignments each put the username into `TraceStep ('caught at '+$step)` and into the error receipt's `step` field, and all survive: `$Step=[string]$system.UserName` (M01), `$local:step=...` (M02), `foreach($step in @([string]$system.UserName)) { }` (M03), `New-Variable -Name step -Value (...) -Force` (M04).
- A lowercase `add-content` writer to an obfuscated trace path (M06) also survives.
findings.suggested_fix:
Make these checks case-insensitive and count every use of `step`.
- Add `re.IGNORECASE` to the TraceStep call, count and `\s+[-"@]` regexes, to the two `$step` assignment regexes, and to the writer and Set-Content deny-lists. Compare case-folded text.
- Count every case-insensitive occurrence of the identifier `step` in the attestor code (whole-line comments removed), for example `len(re.findall(r"(?i)(?<![A-Za-z])step(?![\w-])", code)) == 23` at the current bytes.

I checked both against the current bytes. The case-insensitive calls regex finds 14 calls instead of 13 under M21/M22. The identifier count is 24 instead of 23 under M01-M04/M20. The current source passes both.

verdict.reasoning:
The test gap is real, but nothing wrong is in the current source, so it does not block.

**The finding holds.** In `test_attestor_trace_lines_carry_only_step_names_and_timestamps` (scripts/tests/test_windows11_guest_driver.py, around lines 1407-1440), every guard is a case-sensitive regex or substring check. That includes the `TraceStep` call regex, the `TraceStep` count, the two `$step` assignment regexes, the writer deny-list and the `$script:step` / `Set-Variable` / `[ref]$step` / `${step}` forbidden list. In Windows PowerShell 5.1, function, cmdlet and variable names are case-insensitive. So `Tracestep` and `tracestep` call `TraceStep`, `$Step=` assigns `$step`, and `add-content` is `Add-Content`. The other forms the deny-list misses also change `$step` at top-level script scope:
- `$local:step=`
- `foreach($step in ...)`, whose loop variable keeps its last value after the loop
- `New-Variable -Name step -Force`

I copied the sources to the scratch folder (scratchpad/fix6/review-tests-f1) and ran the test file against each mutant in the finding:
- Baseline: 35 passed.
- M22 (`Tracestep` with the `DefaultPassword` value), M21, M01, M02, M03, M04 and M06: each still 35 passed.
- A control mutant using exact-case `TraceStep ([string]$system.UserName)` was caught (1 failed).

So the test's own comment, which claims every use of `TraceStep`, every write and every `$step` assignment is covered, is not enforced. The suggested fix also checks out on the current bytes: the case-insensitive call regex finds 13 calls, and the case-insensitive count of the `step` identifier, with comment lines removed, is 23.

**Why it is not blocking:**
1. **No leak today.** The current attestor sends no secret, registry value or read value to the trace. Every `TraceStep` argument is a fixed literal or `$step`, and every `$step` assignment is a fixed literal.
2. **Any change is already gated.** `windows11_bootstrap.ps1` and `windows11_guest.ps1` are SHA-256-pinned in `WINDOWS11_NATIVE_PINS` in check_portability.py. Any attestor edit, including these mutants, fails the portability gate until someone deliberately re-pins it.
3. **The username part is not a new class of leak.** The username already reaches the retained proof through the `machine-error.json` message (`'...observed user: '+[string]$system.UserName`), which is unchanged from HEAD. Only the `DefaultPassword` mutant (M22) would be a new leak, and only after a hypothetical future edit.
4. **None of the blocking criteria apply.** The campaign does not accept a wrong result, leak data, hang beyond its bounds, or fail a repository gate. The new tests weaken nothing; they are simply less complete than their comment claims.

It is still worth fixing with `re.IGNORECASE` plus a total `step` identifier count, because it is a known PowerShell trap and cheap to close.

findings.claim: The test for the 10-minute task limit, the KI-0175 fix itself, can be bypassed. Setting the limit back to one minute through a property assignment or a later Set-ScheduledTask still passes all 35 tests.
findings.evidence:
The test checks:
- `settings = re.findall(r"(?m)^\$settings = (.+)$", BOOTSTRAP)`
- `assert BOOTSTRAP.count("New-ScheduledTaskSettingsSet") == 1`
- `assert BOOTSTRAP.count("-ExecutionTimeLimit") == 1`
- `assert "-Settings $settings" in BOOTSTRAP`

Two mutants survive:
- M05 adds `$settings.ExecutionTimeLimit = 'PT1M'` after the `$settings = ...` line.
- M18 adds `$settings.ExecutionTimeLimit='PT1M'; Set-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'JappOwnedMachineAttestation' -Settings $settings | Out-Null` after Register-ScheduledTask.
findings.suggested_fix: Also assert `len(re.findall(r"(?i)ExecutionTimeLimit", BOOTSTRAP)) == 1`. It is 1 now and 2 under M05/M18. Also assert that `Set-ScheduledTask` does not appear (case-insensitive), and pin how often `$settings` is used.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding holds against the current source. In test_attestor_task_limit_is_ten_minutes_beyond_the_guest_wait (scripts/tests/test_windows11_guest_driver.py lines 1311-1326), the only guards are:
- a regex match on the single `^$settings = ...` line;
- `BOOTSTRAP.count("New-ScheduledTaskSettingsSet") == 1`;
- `BOOTSTRAP.count("-ExecutionTimeLimit") == 1`, which needs the leading dash;
- a substring check for `-Settings $settings`.
None of these stops a later change to the limit.

I copied the sources into a scratch tree at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-tanishkalwad-jobapplyv2/17ee071f-b2d5-4e6f-a57e-209b35ae06c1/scratchpad/fix6/review-tests-F2/ and ran the full test file (35 test IDs) against four mutants:
- M05: `$settings.ExecutionTimeLimit = 'PT1M'` after the settings line.
- M18: `$settings.ExecutionTimeLimit='PT1M'; Set-ScheduledTask ... -Settings $settings` after Register-ScheduledTask.
- A variant that assigns `New-TimeSpan -Minutes 1`.
- A lowercase property assignment.
All four passed 35/35, the same as the unmodified tree.

These are valid regressions in Windows PowerShell 5.1. The object from New-ScheduledTaskSettingsSet is a CIM MSFT_TaskSettings instance, and its ExecutionTimeLimit string property can be assigned (for example 'PT1M'). So the test that pins the KI-0175 fix does not catch these rewrites.

The suggested fix fits the current file. A case-insensitive count of ExecutionTimeLimit is 1 now and 2 under the mutants, and Set-ScheduledTask does not appear anywhere today.

This is not blocking. The shipped bootstrap correctly sets 10 minutes (line 99) and registers with `-Settings $settings` (line 100), so the campaign cannot accept a wrong result, leak data or hang from this gap. There is also a second guard: check_portability.py WINDOWS11_NATIVE_PINS pins the bootstrap's exact SHA-256 (a188d35e..., which matches the current file). Both mutants change the hash (63c5c237... and 251f44d6...), so the repository portability gate fails unless someone also re-pins the file. That pin only checks that the file is the reviewed one; it does not check what the file means. A reviewed change that re-pins would still pass the tests silently. The gap is real test weakness in the meaning-level test, not a defect that breaks a gate or the campaign.

findings.claim: `test_machine_receipt_wait_is_150_seconds_inside_the_guest_deadline` does not check what its name and comment say ("never an extension"). Its budget assertion compares two hardcoded numbers. The guest's machine wait is the only clock wait not capped at 300 s, and its loop never calls WithinBudget.
findings.evidence:
- The test asserts `assert int(budget.group(1)) == 300` and then `assert int(budget.group(1)) - 150 >= 150`. Since 150 is a literal in the test, the second line is always true.
- The guest computes `$machineLimit=$clock.Elapsed.TotalSeconds+150` (windows11_guest.ps1:347). Its sibling waits use `$limit=[Math]::Min(300,$clock.Elapsed.TotalSeconds+6)` (lines 146/156/171/181) or `[Math]::Min(300, $clock.Elapsed.TotalSeconds+35)` (line 87), and call WithinBudget inside the loop.
- Mutant M19 inserts `Start-Sleep -Seconds 200` after `$machineSchema=...`, so the wait would end around 350 s, past the 300 s budget. It passes all 35 tests.
- In practice, how far the wait can run past 300 s depends on how long the guest takes to reach it (manifest hashing, Add-Type, CIM), and nothing checks that time.
findings.suggested_fix: Either cap the wait like its siblings, with `[Math]::Min(300,$clock.Elapsed.TotalSeconds+150)` or a WithinBudget call in the loop, and pin that form. Or reword the test name and comment so they do not claim the wait is enforced inside the deadline, and drop the always-true arithmetic.

verdict.reasoning:
The narrow point holds, but the finding overstates it.

Confirmed against the current source:
- In test_machine_receipt_wait_is_150_seconds_inside_the_guest_deadline, the line `assert int(budget.group(1)) == 300` comes first, so the next line, `assert int(budget.group(1)) - 150 >= 150`, can never fail. It adds no checking. The comment above it, "Half the deadline stays ... after the latest receipt the wait accepts", is only true if the wait starts at elapsed 0. The wait actually starts at elapsed T, after the identity check, hashing the four manifest files (the portable zip among them), Add-Type and the CIM query. So the latest accepted receipt leaves 150-T seconds, not 150.
- The guest sets `$machineLimit=$clock.Elapsed.TotalSeconds+150` (windows11_guest.ps1:347). It is not capped with `[Math]::Min(300,...)`, and the do/while loop never calls WithinBudget.
- I reproduced mutant M19 in scratch: inserting `Start-Sleep -Seconds 200` after `$machineSchema=...` still passes all 35 tests in test_windows11_guest_driver.py.

Refuted or overstated:
- "The only clock wait not capped at 300 s" is false. The crash-phase wait, `$until=$clock.Elapsed.TotalSeconds+6` (line 447), is also uncapped and has no WithinBudget call. The dxdiag WaitEmpty(45000) and HostAccepted(15000/60000) bounds also ignore the 300 s mark. Throughout the guest, 300 s is a deadline checked at certain points, not a hard cap, so the uncapped wait follows an existing pattern.
- There is a reasonable reading under which the test does check "part of the guest's own fixed work deadline, never an extension". It pins a single `$clock` Stopwatch created before `$machineLimit`. The wait uses that clock. WithinBudget stays at exactly 300 on the same clock. So the wait's time counts against the 300 s budget, and the budget was not raised to make room for it.
- M19 would fail a repository gate: check_portability.py WINDOWS11_NATIVE_PINS pins the exact sha256 of windows11_guest.ps1, so the mutant does not get through.

Impact, and why this is non-blocking:
- The wait always ends by T+150 s, so it cannot hang. T would have to exceed 150 s for the wait to run past 300 s, and the pre-wait work comes nowhere near that.
- If the guest does overrun, the WithinBudget call at the next Launch throws, so the run fails closed.
- The host's own WORK_SECONDS of 3300 s bounds the campaign.
- No wrong result can be accepted, no data leaks, and no gate fails.

What is left is a test-quality problem: an assertion that can never fail, and a comment that overclaims.
